publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Sept 29: Today's meeting of the House of Representatives has passed the 'Bill to Revive Provisions of Some Nepal Acts, 2083'.

Amendment would be registered on the bill, passed unanimously after discussions on its principles, and further debate would be held on the bill after sending it to the concerned committee.

The government brought this bill after some provisions of the Some Nepal Acts amended from the ordinance expired.

Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, Sobita Gautam, on the behalf of Prime Minister Balendra Shah presented a proposal seeking consideration on the bill.

Taking part in the discussion on the proposal, lawmakers Sushila Dhakal stressed the bill should maintain legal stability raising above political interests while Sajida Khatun Siddqui shared that there should be clear about law enforcement agencies and deadline.

Similarly, HoR members--Yashuda Kumari Baral, Aren Rai, Dr Lalita Kumari, Tuka Bhadra Hamal, Dr Pushpa Raj Kandel, Balawati Sharma, and Parbati BK among others took part in the discussion.

Responding to queries raised in course of discussion, Minister Gautam shared that the government presented the bill as per the policy-level decision of restoring clauses of some Nepal Acts that were expired due to ordinance.(RSS)

title: Warming Himalayas: Nepal’s climate justice test - Eco-Business
description: Warming Himalayas: Nepal’s climate justice test  Eco-Business
publisher.title: Eco-Business
full_article:
The recent floods in Nepal have exposed the growing vulnerability of Himalayan communities and the widening gap between the scale of climate losses and international support.

The devastating Himalayan disaster of 26 August 2026, has left Nepal facing enormous reconstruction costs. The critical question for the global community then is: will climate finance be treated as a matter of justice, instead of charity?

The high-altitude glacier collapse in the northern part of Langtang/Lirung Mountain caused a rock Himalayan tsunami that killed more than 1,451 people as of 19 September 2026, left 5,786 missing and affected about 1.6 million people in five districts of Nepal, according to the government’s situation report.

The government has rescued 13,784 people and mobilised security forces for rescue operations. It assessed damage to 41 motorable bridges, 3,702 private houses, roads and 12 hydropower projects.

The recently released Rapid Damage and Need Assessment (RDNA) estimates total damage and losses at more than US$2.66 billion. About US$4.72 billion is required for reconstruction and rehabilitation, while US$5.7 million is needed for immediate relief and short-term rehabilitation over the next six months.

The flood damaged 7,570 private houses, 48 public buildings, 18 schools, seven health facilities and 30 cultural heritage sites. About $685 million will be required to rehabilitate the social sector.

“ The disaster gives Nepal an opportunity to raise concerns about climate change at the global and regional levels. Communities living in river basins and near glacier lakes remain at high risk.

But the cost of physical damage does not capture the full social impact. Children, women and senior citizens have suffered severe psychosocial impact, while marginalised communities have become further marginalised. These “costs” have been undermined or overlooked in the assessment report.

Scientists working with World Weather Attribution (WWA) described the disaster as a “catastrophic rock-ice avalanche that transitioned into a debris flood in the Himalayas along the Nepal-China border”. They said climate change and rising temperatures in the Himalayan region contributed significantly to the disaster. Floods in the Himalayan region have become more frequent and more devastating in recent years.

The Government of Nepal has written to the Loss and Damage Fund, seeking reparation for the impacts of climate change and calling on polluters to provide compensation and justice. The Loss and Damage Fund said Nepal should provide sufficient evidence about the causes of the flood. Its board will consider providing up to US$20 million in compensation.

Compared with the estimated losses, the proposed support is small. The World Bank has also offered concessional loans to Nepal. Members of the civil society and youth are demanding grants as reparation rather than loans. They have been demanding climate justice, focusing on the causes of glacier melt in the Himalayas, known as the “Third Pole” and a source of water for large numbers of people in the region.

Campaigners argue that the climate crisis is a fundamental human rights issue linked to the right to life and a sustainable environment. They are also calling for climate finance to be treated as justice rather than charity and for a regional framework across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region to share information, establish early-warning systems and develop institutional mechanisms.

Ten young people began a hunger strike on 18 September 2026, at the base camp of Mount Manaslu. They are demanding assessments of future glacial lake outburst flood risks, regular joint monitoring of lakes along the China-Nepal border, and climate compensation and justice for Nepal, which has to bear the costs of climate-related impacts to which it has not contributed.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah is due to attend the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, where he will raise the issue of the climate crisis impacting Nepal. It is an opportunity for Nepal to present the context and causes of the recent disaster internationally. Foreign Minister Sisir Khanal has already left for the UNGA and is due to attend side events in New York. He is also expected to appeal for international support to overcome the crisis.

Civil society and the public have raised concerns about delays in rescuing people trapped in a hydropower tunnel, saying the government did not allow international experts to assist during the early phase of the rescue. They have also raised concerns about delays in search operations.

Nepal will need to amplify its demands for climate justice, including through the Loss and Damage Fund, while ensuring accountability and transparency in the use of funds. The federal government’s initial hesitation to collaborate with local governments also created tensions between federal and provincial governments.

The internally displaced are being housed in 27 holding centres in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, where 1,743 people are living. The government has offered US$98 (NPR 15,000) per family member to stay outside the holding centres for four months.

The disaster gives Nepal an opportunity to raise concerns about climate change at the global and regional levels. Communities living in river basins and near glacier lakes remain at high risk. Nepal should seek timely information-sharing from the international community to reduce those risks, while international partners can provide technology for faster warnings.

Existing early-warning technology and knowledge may not be sufficient to predict disasters of this kind. Investment is, therefore, needed not only for recovery but also for research and knowledge exchange. Digital technology and empowered communities could help reduce vulnerabilities.

Nepal also needs people-centred development to cope with such disasters, including the exchange of knowledge on infrastructure capable of withstanding harsh Himalayan conditions. Nepal, China and India need to minimise human activities that directly or indirectly affect the ecology and environment of the Himalayas.

Community-led initiatives, respect for indigenous knowledge and participation in development could help sustain the region’s ecology and reduce degradation.

Small states such as Nepal need global support to rebuild after large-scale disasters. The Government of Nepal also needs to prioritise community rebuilding in future interventions rather than focusing on the business community.

Som Niroula is a research scholar at the Department of Conflict, Peace and Development, Tribhuvan University, Kathmandu, Nepal. He is also a member of the CRG Research Collective, Calcutta, and was a Junior Fellow at Institut für die Wissenschaften vom Menschen, Vienna.

title: Charity appeal sends solar equipment to flood-affected Nepal - pv magazine Global
description: Charity appeal sends solar equipment to flood-affected Nepal  pv magazine Global
publisher.title: pv magazine Global
full_article:
UK-based charity One Kind Act says the first batch of solar equipment delivered under its fundraiser for communities impacted by flash floods in Nepal has been dispatched.

The charity launched an appeal titled Solar power for Nepal flood victims following floods on August 26 that swept through the mountainous regions of Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, destroying homes and critical infrastructure.

One Kind Act’s fundraiser explains the hydropower facilities and electricity networks the area depends on were badly affected, while damaged roads and river crossings mean repairing this infrastructure will prove difficult and slow.

The funds raised by the charity’s action is going towards sending solar PV equipment to the region in order to create local power installations where electricity is urgently required, such as medical centres and villages.

“For villages that may remain disconnected from the grid for weeks or months, solar power offers a practical and rapidly deployable solution,” the charity’s fundraiser explains.

“Solar panels and supporting equipment can be transported into remote areas without the continuing fuel requirements of generators, providing communities with an independent source of essential electricity while permanent infrastructure is restored.”

According to a social media post, the first batch of solar equipment has left Delhi, India, and is on its way to Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu.

One Kind Act’s update says this first batch is expected to provide emergency solar power support to approximately 50 clusters of 10 households each, equating to around 500 households in total.

The charity’s fundraiser has raised GBP 4,022 ($5,323.70) to date. Its website lists a closing date for donations of November 30.

title: Himlung Himal Avalanche in Nepal Buries 16 Climbers at Base Camp - SnowBrains
description: Himlung Himal Avalanche in Nepal Buries 16 Climbers at Base Camp  SnowBrains
publisher.title: SnowBrains
full_article:
Himlung Himal Base Camp. The mountain is one of the easier 7,000-meter peaks in the area, a good testing ground for beginner mountaineers. Photo: Magical Summits

Disaster has struck Nepal’s Himalayan region once again, as an avalanche has buried 16 people — mostly climbers and support staff — at the Himlung Himal base camp in Nepal. The group reached base camp early to help set up operations and ropes ahead of expedition teams. Following heavy precipitation across a broad swath of the region, an immense avalanche buried the camp under 14 feet (4 meters) of debris.

Rescue operations have recovered the bodies of four of the dead. Rescuers found two on Sunday, September 27, and two more on Monday, September 28, 2026. Meanwhile, rescuers believe 12 more staff remain buried beneath the debris, though operations have paused because of the scale of the required manual digging and ongoing severe weather and mountain conditions. Within hours of the avalanche, a fresh layer of snow already covered the debris.

Related: Nims Dai Purja Confirmed Dead Following Broad Peak Avalanche in Pakistan

View this post on Instagram

An Entry-Level Climb

Himlung Himal, at 23,380 feet (7,126 meters), is one of the least technical 7,000-ers, considered a great entry-level climb for aspiring mountaineers. In fact, despite the recent disaster, the normal route is relatively safe from objective hazards by Himalayan standards and has a very high summit rate. According to a Nepal National Mountain Guide Association (NNMGA) Instagram update, “the avalanche was enormous — no one had believed that Himlung Base Camp could experience something of that scale.”

A Year of Misfortune in the Himalaya

The Himlung Himal avalanche is the latest in a series of disasters for Nepal. On July 30, 2026, legendary mountaineer Nims Dai Purja died in an avalanche on Broad Peak, along with nine others. At the end of August, a massive landslide triggered a flash flood that enveloped an entire river valley in a matter of minutes, killing 1,400 people and leaving more than 6,000 still missing.

More recently, two climbers died in a slab avalanche on Manaslu, just 16 miles (25 kilometers) as the crow flies from Himlung Himal. With more severe weather expected, authorities closed the mountain shortly thereafter. A massive rescue effort followed, evacuating more than 1,000 climbers and guides by helicopter.

Related: How a Landslide Triggered a Biblical Flash Flood in Tibet and Nepal

Since then, flooding in Nepal and northeast India has been extensive. The same storms that have abruptly ended the Manaslu climbing season have also produced severe flooding in India’s Himachal Pradesh province, killing over 60 people as of September 29.

While any year can bring unusual weather patterns, climate scientists and meteorologists are particularly worried about this year’s record El Niño. El Niño is the warm phase of the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO). Historically, it has signaled severe weather across the globe. The 1877-78 El Niño resulted in the deaths of an estimated 50 million people — about 3-4% of the entire global population at the time — largely due to changes in monsoonal rains in Asia.

Fortunately, with immense technological advances, we’re unlikely to experience anything close to that level of human mortality. However, experts agree that this year will almost certainly produce unusually destructive natural disasters. Likewise, those with mountain pursuits in mind should expect unusual weather and avalanche scenarios and adjust their decision-making accordingly.

title: The floods swept away Nepal’s China bet; India remains important - firstpost.com
description: The floods swept away Nepal’s China bet; India remains important  firstpost.com
publisher.title: firstpost.com
full_article:
On August 26, a chunk of ice broke off a glacier, sending a torrent of mud, water and ice through the banks of the Trishuli River, also known as the Bhotekoshi, which runs between China and Nepal. The deluge obliterated the Gyirong Port complex at Rasuwagadhi-Timure — Nepal’s primary overland gateway to China. The death toll from the catastrophic flash floods in Nepal topped 1,400 people with over 6,100 more still missing, as per the country's disaster management authorities.

Reconstructing the severed transit infrastructure alone is projected to cost several millions of dollars. Nepal's authorities estimate the damage from the recent floods will exceed $5 billion. The destruction has left the landlocked nation without a functioning land route to China. The flash floods also destroyed the Miteri Bridge connecting Nepal with China, along with houses, roads, and entire villages. The deluge also destroyed hydropower infrastructure, damaging multiple projects and reducing Nepal’s total power generation by at least 10 per cent.

Advertisement

Advertisement

For years, Nepal framed the northern trade corridor as a way to reduce its dependence on India: a direct gateway to China, the world’s second-largest economy. Yet the recent deluge has exposed how much of that corridor was built on political symbolism rather than resilient infrastructure. Today, amid the collapse of the northern crossings, what remains standing fully functional is the economic and geographical reliance on India that Nepal's policymakers long insisted they needed to outgrow.

More from Opinion

The loss of the Rasuwagadhi-Timure crossing severs Nepal's primary artery to the north. The nation’s other historic border post at Kodari-Zhangmu has remained dysfunctional since the 2015 earthquake. With Rasuwagadhi now crippled, Kathmandu doesn't possess working land access to its northern neighbour.

Rebuilding critical infrastructure through volatile terrain will take years, and Beijing’s track record on Himalayan engineering timelines offers scant grounds for optimism. Meanwhile, Indian border checkpoints at Birgunj and Biratnagar remain fully operational, absorbing the trade momentum of the Himalayan nation.

The trade through Rasuwagadhi was never as substantial as the political theatre surrounding it suggested. While China remains Nepal's second-largest source of imports, it buys almost nothing in return. By contrast, India is Nepal's largest trading partner, accounting for about 64 per cent of Nepal's total external trade, according to a data. Nepal’s economy was never genuinely balanced between its two giant neighbours; it was fully anchored to India.

Advertisement

Advertisement

Emergency supplies, heavy construction material, fuel, and the machinery required to rebuild the destroyed districts of Rasuwa and Nuwakot will move on Indian-linked roads and through Indian ports. This is the only network capable of moving that volume into Nepal at speed, right now, without waiting for bureaucratic clearance from Beijing. The same reality governs remittances, which continue to flow from more than a million Nepali workers in India, providing a critical lifeline to households in the flood-affected districts. Crisis has a violent way of stripping away strategic hedging, forcing nations to lean on the relationships that actually deliver.

This does not mean abandoning Chinese investment outright, or pretending that Kathmandu has no interest in a functioning northern corridor someday. But realistic policy must reckon with what geology just did to that ambition. The very mountains that were supposed to open an alternative major market instead confirmed what geography and economics had already settled that northern corridor was always the harder, slower, less certain route.

Rivers can be rerouted, given sufficient time and capital, but a trade relationship built on genuine market demand cannot be manufactured overnight, no matter how many bridges are rebuilt. For Kathmandu, the latest economic disruption serves as a costly reminder of which neighbour offers a true partnership.

(Brabim Karki is a columnist and commentator who writes for international publications including The Independent, Nikkei Asia, South China Morning Post, The Hill, Hindustan Times, The Economic Times, The Indian Express, CNN-News18, The Japan Times, and The Straits Times. title: Second National Conservation Forum concluded in Nepal - International Union for Conservation of Nature
description: Second National Conservation Forum concluded in Nepal  International Union for Conservation of Nature
publisher.title: International Union for Conservation of Nature
full_article:
The forum was inaugurated by the Honourable Minister of Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment (MoAFE), Government of Nepal, Ms Geeta Chaudhary, who emphasised the importance of international cooperation and cross-border coordination for biodiversity conservation. "Wildlife movement, river flows, ecological systems and ecosystem services do not recognize administrative boundaries. Therefore, the benefits of conservation are not confined within the boundaries, and we must therefore promote landscape level conservation and pursue nature-based solutions that transcend administrative borders." She also highlighted the government's commitment to integrating conservation efforts with sustainable development.

Honourable Minister of Ministry of Agriculture, Forests and Environment, Geeta Chaudhary delivering inagural speech

In a recorded message, Dr Dindo Campilan, Regional Hub Director for Asia and Oceania, IUCN, highlighted the importance of the Forum in bringing stakeholders together and responding to growing pressures on nature . “Nepal’s biodiversity and natural resources have outstanding value, locally, nationally and universally. Yet these are under increasing pressure from climate change, habitat loss, unsustainable use of natural resources, and other human-driven pressures,” he said.

Dr Yoji Natori, Acting Chair of IUCN Asia Regional Members Committee (ARMC), highlighted the role of the ARMC and noted that the outcomes of the forum could be further shared at the next ARMC meeting. "A well discussed plan and the execution of the well-planned activities at the national level will make the dialogue at the regional level more meaningful," he said.

Dr Yoji Natori Acting Chair of IUCN ARMC delivering the speech

The Secretary of MoAFE, Dr Rajendra Prasad Mishra, IUCN Regional Councillor for South and East Asia Ms Roshani Adhikari Pathak and IUCN Nepal Country Representative Dr Narendra Man Babu Pradhan also wished the success of the event through their inaugural speeches. The session was chaired by the chairperson of IUCN Nepal National Committee Mr Kiran Timalsina.

Two keynote presentations on 'Human-Wildlife Coexistence' and 'Climate Finance' were presented during the inaugural session by Dr Ghana Shyam Gurung, WWF Nepal and Dr Manish Raj Pandey, NTNC respectively.

Following the inaugural session, more than a dozen plenary and parallel thematic sessions were held to discuss and address Nepal’s most critical conservation and socio-ecological frontiers over the two days.

High-level policy and field evidence sessions focused on rising human-wildlife conflict, including wild Asian elephants, human-tiger interactions in shared landscapes, Himalayan black bear hotspots, and snow leopard conservation and landscape management. Experts also highlighted the urgent need to bridge the biodiversity finance gap, strengthen forest carbon trading mechanisms, and ensure direct and accessible climate and disaster financing for vulnerable mountain and local communities.

The forum further explored emerging threats to freshwater ecosystems and river corridors alongside the conservation of neglected and endangered species such as the Chinese pangolin and mid-hill stream frogs. The experts also discussed the interconnected issues on climate, disaster and financing, illegal wildlife and pet trade, the future of Community Forestry over the next decade, bio-utilization approaches for managing invasive alien species, and opportunities to promote green corporate investment. The collective discussions and recommendations from these sessions were consolidated into the Forum outcome, outlining shared priorities and commitments for advancing biodiversity conservation, climate resilience and sustainable natural resource management in Nepal.
